title: The recipe nobody asked you to change
hook: Pepsi wins the taste test. Do you change a 99-year-old recipe?

profit.label: Sales
profit.hint: How much cola you sell today

future.label: Loyalty
future.hint: How much your fans love and trust Coke

intro.text: It is 1984. Coca-Cola is the best-selling soft drink in the world, and its formula has barely changed in nearly 100 years. But for 15 years in a row, your lead over your biggest rival has been shrinking. Since 1975, Pepsi has run the Pepsi Challenge: people taste two colas without seeing the names, and more of them pick Pepsi.

d1.title: Why are we losing?
d1.setup: Your own blind tests say the same thing as Pepsi's: people like a sweeter taste. While making Diet Coke, which you launched in 1982, your lab also found a sweeter recipe that beat both Pepsi and your own Coke.
d1.question: What do you do about the slide?
d1.advisor: Pepsi says the problem is your taste. Is that the whole story, or just their story?

options.label: Work in secret on a sweeter new recipe for Coke.
options.outcome: Coca-Cola decided that the taste was the problem. A secret team, code-named Project Kansas, worked on a new, sweeter formula. In taste tests with nearly 200,000 people, it beat both Pepsi and the old Coke.
options.why: Testing new tastes is fair. But people buy Coke for habit and memories too, not only for one sip. Your team was now set on changing the main drink.
options.better: Keep the old recipe safe. Win with new drinks and fresh ads, the way Diet Coke did, and test new tastes as extra drinks.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you treated a fight about feelings as a fight about flavour.

options.label: Keep the recipe. Win with new drinks and fresh ads, like Diet Coke.
options.outcome: Our estimate: your old Coke stays the same, and new drinks bring in new buyers. Fresh ads remind people why they love Coke. Pepsi still wins some taste tests, but your fans stay loyal.
options.why: Your recipe was not your only strength. Your name, your history and your fans' habits were worth more than one sip in a blind test.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you grew around your core product instead of changing it.

options.label: Cut prices to win buyers back from Pepsi.
options.outcome: Our estimate: Pepsi cuts its prices too. Both of you earn less on every bottle, and shoppers start to think of cola as a cheap drink. Your share barely moves.
options.why: A price war hurts both sides, and the stronger brand loses the most. It also tells fans your drink is worth less.
options.better: Protect your price. Give people new reasons to choose Coke, like new drinks and fresh ads.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you fought with discounts and made your own drink look cheap.

d2.title: The taste test winner

setup.text: The new, sweeter formula won the taste tests. But the tests asked about taste, not about how people would feel if their old Coke was gone. About 10 to 12 in every 100 testers said they were angry at the idea of a change, and might stop drinking Coke.
Our estimate: your lab still works on a sweeter recipe, and it beats Pepsi in blind tests. But some testers say they would be angry if their old Coke went away.

d2.question: What do you do with the new recipe?
d2.advisor: A taste test tells you what people sip. It does not tell you what they love.

options.label: Launch it as a new drink, and keep the old Coke on every shelf.
options.outcome: Our estimate: the sweet new drink gets lots of attention, and nobody loses the Coke they grew up with. Pepsi has nothing to laugh at.
options.why: You got the upside of the new taste without taking anything away from your fans.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you added a new choice instead of taking away an old one.

options.label: Replace the old Coke with the new recipe everywhere.
options.outcome: On April 23, 1985, at an event in New York, Coca-Cola announced its first new formula in 99 years. The old recipe was taken off the market. Pepsi gave its staff a day off and ran full-page newspaper ads.
options.why: You took away something millions of people loved, and you trusted a sip test more than their feelings. The warning signs were in your own research.
options.better: Sell the new taste as an extra drink, or test it in a few cities first, and never take the old one away.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you took away what fans loved because a test said they would like something else.

options.label: Sell it in a few cities first and watch how fans react.
options.outcome: Our estimate: in your test cities, some people like the sweet taste, but many are angry that their old Coke is gone. The anger stays small and local, and you learn a lot.
options.why: Testing first was careful. But in those cities you still took away the drink fans loved.
options.better: Launch the new taste as an extra drink, so nobody has to lose the old one.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you tested before going big, but still tested the wrong idea.

d3.title: The fans fight back
d3.setup: Within weeks, angry calls pour in. By June your hotline gets 1,500 calls a day, up from 400. About 40,000 letters arrive. Fans form protest groups, and one says it has signed up 100,000 supporters. Some people buy up all the old Coke they can find. A poll finds only 13 in 100 soda drinkers like the new taste.
d3.question: Your fans are furious. What do you do?
d3.advisor: Your tests said people love the new taste. Your phones are saying something else.

options.label: Spend big on ads to win fans over to the new taste.
options.outcome: Our estimate: the ads are everywhere, but they cannot change how people feel. Some new buyers try the drink. Your old fans feel you are not listening.
options.why: Ads can tell people about a product. They cannot make people stop missing something they loved.
options.better: Admit the mistake fast. Bring the old recipe back and say sorry.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you tried to out-shout your own customers.

options.label: Wait. People will get used to it in a few months.
options.outcome: Our estimate: the anger does not fade. It grows. Every week brings more news stories, more protests and more Pepsi ads that make fun of you.
options.why: When fans feel something was taken from them, silence looks like you do not care.
options.better: Listen to the fans. Bring the old recipe back quickly and say sorry.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you waited for an angry crowd to calm down, and it got angrier.

options.label: Bring back the old recipe as Coca-Cola Classic, and say sorry.
options.outcome: On July 11, 1985, 79 days after the change, the company said sorry and brought back the old recipe as Coca-Cola Classic. TV news broke into regular shows to report it. The company's hotline got 31,600 calls in two days.
options.why: Saying sorry is hard for a big company. But you listened, moved within weeks, and gave fans back what they loved.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you admitted a big mistake fast and fixed it.

d3alt.title: What the test told you

setup.text: Our estimate: the sweet new drink sits on shelves next to the old Coke. Some people like it, but most still reach for the taste they grew up with.
Our estimate: in your test cities, many fans are angry that their old Coke is gone. Others like the sweet taste.

d3alt.question: What next for the sweet recipe?
d3alt.advisor: Your fans just told you what matters to them. Did you hear it?

options.label: Replace the old Coke everywhere anyway. The taste tests can't be wrong.
options.outcome: Our estimate: fans across the country get angry, just as your test warned. After a hard summer of protests, you give in and bring the old taste back.
options.why: You had a warning and ignored it. A test is only useful if you act on what it tells you.
options.better: Keep the old Coke as the star, and sell the sweet taste only as a side drink.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you ignored your own warning signs.

options.label: Sell it only in places where buyers liked it.
options.outcome: Our estimate: the sweet drink sells in a few places, but running different Cokes in different places is costly and confusing.
options.why: It was safe, but it split your effort for a small gain.
options.better: Make the old Coke the star everywhere, and keep the sweet taste as a clear side drink.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you played safe, but made your brand more confusing.

options.label: Keep the old Coke as the star. Sell the sweet one as a side drink.
options.outcome: Our estimate: fans keep the Coke they love, and the sweet drink finds its own small group of buyers. Your lead over Pepsi starts to grow again.
options.why: You listened to what the test really said: people liked the new taste, but loved the old Coke.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you kept your core safe and let the new idea earn its place.

d4.title: Two Cokes on one shelf

setup.text: The old recipe is back as Coca-Cola Classic. Now two Cokes share the shelf: Classic, and the new, sweeter one.
Our estimate: your ads did not change many minds. By autumn you give in and bring the old recipe back. Now two Cokes share the shelf.
Our estimate: the anger did not fade. By autumn you give in and bring the old recipe back, months late. Now two Cokes share the shelf.
Our estimate: your old Coke and the sweet new drink now share the shelf.

d4.question: How do you run two colas at once?
d4.advisor: Two drinks can mean two chances. Or two ways to confuse people.

options.label: Make the old Coke the star, and let the new drink fade quietly.
options.outcome: Our estimate: all your money and attention go behind the taste fans love. The new drink slowly leaves the shelves, and nobody misses it much.
options.why: You put your effort where your fans already were, and stopped spending on a drink they did not want.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you backed what your customers chose, not what you hoped they would choose.

options.label: Keep both, and give each one its own big ad campaign.

outcome.text: Coca-Cola kept both drinks and gave each one its own ad campaign. Classic quickly outsold the new drink, and within a few months it was again the top sugar cola, ahead of Pepsi. The new drink fell to about 3% of the market. It was later renamed Coke II, and it was dropped in 2002.
Our estimate: you pay for two sets of ads. The old Coke wins most buyers, and the sweet drink slowly shrinks.

options.why: Keeping both was safe, but you spent money and attention on a drink few people wanted.
options.better: Put your weight behind the taste fans chose, and let the new drink fade quietly.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you split your effort between a winner and a loser.

options.label: Push the new Coke as your main brand. Classic is just for old fans.
options.outcome: Our estimate: fans feel you still do not get it. They buy Classic anyway, and the money you spend on the new drink is wasted.
options.why: You fought your own customers a second time, after they had already told you what they wanted.
options.better: Back the drink your fans chose, and let the new one fade.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you kept pushing a product your customers had already rejected.

legend.title: The taste that never left
legend.text: Our estimate: you never took your fans' favourite drink away. New drinks and fresh ads bring in new buyers, and Coke's lead over Pepsi grows again without a summer of anger.

text.text: By the end of 1985, Coca-Cola Classic was selling well ahead of both the new drink and Pepsi. The sweeter recipe became a small side drink and was dropped in 2002. In 2009 the word Classic came off the label in North America: it was just Coca-Cola again. Coca-Cola came out of the mess stronger, after learning in public how much its fans loved the old taste.
Our estimate: you made some costly moves, but you listened in time. Your fans stay with you, and Coke stays ahead of Pepsi.

collapse.title: The cola that lost its fans
collapse.text: Our estimate: you fought your own customers for too long. Many of them switch to Pepsi for good, and the world's best-known drink loses its lead.

fired.title: The board lets you go
fired.text: Our estimate: three costly calls in a row. The board has lost its trust in you, and asks someone else to win the fans back.

realHistory: Coca-Cola was losing ground to Pepsi, which kept winning blind taste tests. After tests with nearly 200,000 people, it replaced its 99-year-old recipe with a sweeter one on April 23, 1985. Fans were furious: calls, letters and protest groups poured in. After 79 days, on July 11, 1985, the company said sorry and brought back the old recipe as Coca-Cola Classic. Within months Classic was again the top sugar cola, ahead of Pepsi. The new drink fell to about 3% of the market and was dropped in 2002.
